1226.title: Medicine
1226.hook: Luke the beloved physician, a Samaritan with oil and wine: Christians see healing by doctors as God's work too
1226.howItsDone: Christians pray for the sick and for those who treat them; churches run hospitals, clinics and nursing ministries, and some keep a feast of Saint Luke, when they remember doctors and pray for healers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hospital hallway and a courtroom, and the hardest choices. Your line was every life counts.

Hospitals carry some telling names. Good Samaritan. Mercy. Saint Luke's. That last name belongs to a man the New Testament names only in passing. In a greeting at the end of one of Paul's letters, he's called "Luke, the beloved physician." Tradition says this is the same Luke who wrote a Gospel and the book of Acts. A doctor, standing right in the middle of the early church's story, and nobody in it seems to think that's strange. Today: medicine.

Jesus himself reaches for the doctor when he describes his own work. Criticized for eating with sinners, he answers: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick." He doesn't treat the physician as a rival to God. He uses the physician as the picture. Then there's the Good Samaritan, whose name ended up on hospitals too. Look at what he actually does on that road. He "bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine." That's first aid, the medicine of the day. Then he brings the man to an inn, pays, and tells the innkeeper, "Take care of him." Emergency care, then ongoing care, with the bill covered. One more text, the book of Sirach, sits in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and among the Apocrypha in some Protestant ones. It tells readers to honor the physician, because the Lord created him, and it says the Lord brings medicines out of the earth. Put these together and you get a way of seeing medicine. When someone gets well under a surgeon's hands or a nurse's patience or a pharmacist's careful counting, Christians who see it this way don't call it God's work or the doctor's. They call it both. God heals, and very often God heals through hands. That's why prayer and medicine are allowed to sit in the same room.

Bring to mind one time someone helped you, or someone you love, get well: a doctor who explained things slowly, a nurse on a night shift, a pharmacist who caught a mistake, a parent with a bandage and a steady voice. Let one face come clear, and remember what their hands actually did. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for that person by name; if you don't, just let yourself be grateful to them.
Medicine. For Christians who see it this way, the healing work of doctors, nurses and every careful hand, which they count as God's work too.
Your line: God heals through hands. Every careful hand counts. That's today, done.

1227.title: Attention
1227.hook: what we look at shapes us: Paul's list of things to think on (Philippians 4:8)
1227.howItsDone: Christians practice this through daily scripture reading, times of silence, fasting from media during seasons like Lent, and examining at day's end what they gave their attention to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke the beloved physician, and a Samaritan with oil and wine. Your line was God heals through hands.

Quick question, no wrong answers: what was the last thing you looked at before this lesson started? And the thing before that? And before that? For some of us the trail runs back through a string of small screens, each a few seconds long, none of them chosen exactly. Paul, writing to the church at Philippi while he's in chains, closes his letter with a list. It isn't a list of rules. It's a list of things to look at, and keep looking at, until they shape you. Today: attention.

Here's the list, in the King James Bible: "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things." Notice what kind of list it is: not things to avoid, but things to go looking for. The words think on translate a Greek word for reckoning, the kind of counting a bookkeeper does. Take account of these. Add them up. Jesus says something close in the Sermon on the Mount: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light." In Jesus' picture, what you look at doesn't stay outside you. It gets in. It becomes the light you live by. And because that's hard, the Psalms turn it into a request: "Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity." Guarding your gaze, in this tradition, isn't only willpower. It's something asked for. So Christians who take this seriously do two things at once. They turn away from some things, not out of fear, but because a gaze is limited and the hours are few. And they turn toward something better: a face across the table, a page worth reading, a sky, a true word. Attention is something you give. Paul's question is what you're giving it to.

segments.voice: Put your phone face down, choose one thing in front of you, a window, your own hands, a cup, and look at it as if you'd been asked to describe it to someone who can't see: its color, its edges, where the light lands. When the pull to check something comes, and it may, notice it, and come back. If you pray, you can use the line from the Psalms: "Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity."
Attention. Where you point your eyes and mind: Paul says think on what is true and lovely, and Jesus calls the eye the light of the body.
Your line: guard your gaze. In Jesus' picture, what you look at gets in. See you tomorrow.

1228.title: What forgiveness isn't
1228.hook: forgiving isn't excusing, forgetting, or staying in danger: Luke 17, Joseph, and David at the stronghold
1228.howItsDone: Christians pray "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" in the Lord's Prayer, and pastors and Christian counselors teach that forgiving a wrong does not require excusing it, forgetting it, or remaining in an unsafe relationship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's list from a prison cell: whatsoever things are true. Your line was guard your gaze.

"Just forgive and forget." It gets said in kitchens, over the phone, sometimes to people who are still being hurt. It sounds biblical. It isn't. Those words aren't in the Bible. And when you read what the Bible does say about forgiving, it turns out to be harder than that slogan in one way, and much safer in another. This path met forgiveness early, with a servant who wouldn't pass the mercy on. Today, a short list of what it isn't. It isn't excusing. It isn't forgetting. And it isn't staying in danger.

First, it isn't excusing. Jesus says in Luke: "If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him." The wrong gets named first. Excusing says it wasn't really wrong. Forgiving says it was, and then lets something go. The Greek word behind forgive here is aphiemi, and it means to let go, to release, to send away. It's what you do with a debt. You release the claim, the right to get even. You don't erase the record. Second, it isn't forgetting. At the end of Genesis, Joseph forgives the brothers who sold him into slavery, and he says it plainly: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." He remembers exactly what they did. He forgives with the memory wide open. Third, it isn't staying in danger. In First Samuel, King Saul is hunting David to kill him. David has a chance to kill Saul in a cave, and spares him. Saul weeps and admits David is more righteous than he is. Then the story says Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to the stronghold. David doesn't move back into the palace. He leaves the judging to God, and he keeps his distance. Forgiveness and trust are different things. Trust may come back slowly, or not at all. If someone is hurting you, getting safe is not a failure to forgive; if you're in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

Bring to mind someone who hurt you, not the deepest wound, something middle-sized, and name what they did, plainly, to yourself. Then notice the debt, the wish for them to pay, and see if you can set it down, even partway, while keeping whatever boundary keeps you safe; if this stirs up something heavy, stop, and talk with someone you trust. If you pray, you can use the line from the Lord's Prayer: "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."
What forgiveness isn't. Not calling a wrong right, not erasing the memory, not walking back into harm. It's letting go of the debt.
Your line: forgive and stay safe. Forgiveness and trust are different things. Go gently today.

1229.title: Going to your brother (Matthew 18:15–17)
1229.hook: Jesus' steps for a wrong between people: speak privately first, aiming to win the person back
1229.howItsDone: Christians use Matthew 18:15–17 as a guide for conflict in families, friendships and congregations; some churches build it into their rules for church discipline, and pastors coach members to go to the person privately before involving anyone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what forgiveness isn't: not excusing, not forgetting, not staying in danger. Your line was forgive and stay safe.

Someone close does something that stings. A comment in front of others. A promise quietly dropped. There are two easy moves. One is to tell everyone else: a friend, a sibling, a group chat, anyone except the person who did it. The other is to say nothing and let it sour slowly. Jesus offers a third move, and it may be the hardest of the three, because it goes straight to the one person you'd rather avoid. Yesterday's line still stands: this is for ordinary hurts between people who are safe with each other.

In Matthew 18, Jesus lays out steps, and the order matters. Step one, in the King James Bible: "if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother." Alone. Before anyone else hears about it. And the goal: gained thy brother. Not won the argument; won back the person. Step two, only if step one fails: take one or two others along, "that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established." That phrase comes from the Torah's own rule for fair judgment, in Deuteronomy. The witnesses aren't there to gang up. They're there to keep things fair and clear. Step three: "tell it unto the church." And if he won't hear even the church, Jesus says, "let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." Here readers part ways. Some churches read this as a step of formal discipline: the person is treated as outside the fellowship until they turn back. Other readers notice who is telling the story. The Gospel itself calls its namesake Matthew the publican, a tax collector, and Jesus ate with tax collectors. So they hear it as: start over with them, the way Jesus started with Matthew. Either way, the shape is the same. The circle begins at its smallest. The hope is that it never has to widen. Going privately protects the other person's dignity, and it gives the friendship a real chance.

Bring to mind one hurt from someone you're close to that you've told others about, or swallowed, and picture going to them alone. Find your first sentence, plain and short, what happened and how it landed on you, with no list of old grievances, and say it silently a few times until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can ask for a soft voice and a fair ear.
Going to your brother. Jesus' first step when someone wrongs you: tell them alone, hoping to win them back.
Your line: go privately first. The circle begins at its smallest. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1230.title: Enemies
1230.hook: bring back your enemy's ox: love, do good, bless and pray, from the Torah to Jesus to Paul
1230.howItsDone: Christians pray for their enemies by name in private prayer and in church intercessions, and try to answer hostility with practical kindness, citing Luke 6:27–28 and Romans 12:14–21.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matthew 18: go to the one who hurt you, alone, first. Your line was go privately first.

Tucked among the laws in Exodus is one that sounds oddly specific: "If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again." Not your friend's ox. Your enemy's. The one person whose lost donkey you might quietly enjoy hearing about. And the next verse goes further: if his donkey has collapsed under its load, help him lift it. In the Torah, the law is already asking for this: a small, practical good, done for someone you can't stand. This path first heard love your enemies on day two hundred forty-seven; today, how practical it gets.

Jesus takes that thread and pulls it tight. In Luke's Gospel he says: "Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you." The verbs are practical: love, do good, bless, pray. Most of them are things you do with your hands or your mouth. None of them asks you to pretend the person is your friend. Paul writes it to Rome, as short as he can make it: "Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not." The Greek word for bless there means, at its simplest, to speak well of. So the command is about your words. When the person comes up, in conversation or in your own head, you don't curse them. You speak well, or you wish them well. Then Paul quotes Proverbs: "if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." Readers differ about the coals. Some hear the burn of shame that might turn an enemy around. Others hear something gentler. The first half isn't in doubt: feed him. None of this undoes what came two days ago. Doing good to an enemy isn't the same as walking back into harm. You can send the ox home without moving in with its owner. What these texts ask is narrower and harder: no curses, and one concrete good.

Bring to mind someone you find hard, a rival, a critic, someone who has wronged you, and notice what your mind says about them first, without scolding yourself for it. Then try Paul's turn: wish them one specific good thing, a good night's sleep, a worry that lifts, and hold that wish for a few breaths, even if it feels thin. If you pray, you can do what Jesus asks in Luke and pray for them by name.
Enemies. The people Jesus tells his followers to love, do good to, bless and pray for, starting with one practical good.
Your line: bless, do not curse. To bless is to speak well of. Rest well.

1231.title: Christ and culture
1231.hook: some Christians set themselves apart, some work to change the culture, some live in two kingdoms at once
1231.carry: in the world, not of it
1231.howItsDone: Christians live this out in different ways: some in communities that keep apart from the wider culture, some through work in public life, schools and the arts, and some by teaching two kingdoms, with duties to both church and state.

segments.voice: Yesterday, enemies, and an enemy's ox brought back home. Your line was bless, do not curse.

It's the night before Jesus dies, and in John 17 he prays aloud for his friends. A few verses apart, he says two things about them. "These are in the world," he says. And then: "They are not of the world." Some Christians fold the pair into one short saying: in the world, not of it. Both halves stand. Nobody is taken out, and nobody simply blends in. So how do you live inside that pair of sentences? Christians have worked out different answers.
screen: `IN THE WORLD. NOT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the heart of Jesus' prayer: "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil." Not out. Kept. So the question becomes how. The theologian H. Richard Niebuhr wrote a book called Christ and Culture that sorted Christian answers into types. Three of them are easy to spot. Some Christians set themselves apart. Amish and other Anabaptist communities, and monks and nuns in their own way, draw clear lines between their life and the wider culture, so they can live differently together. They point to Paul: "be not conformed to this world." Some Christians aim to change the culture from inside: in schools, hospitals, laws, art, business. They point to Jesus: "Ye are the salt of the earth." Salt doesn't leave the food. It changes the taste. And some live in two kingdoms at once. Martin Luther taught that God governs in two ways, through the gospel and through the law and sword of rulers, and a Christian lives under both. Christians in this line point to Jesus, asked about paying taxes: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's." Each has its scriptures, its saints and its honest arguments, and this path won't rank them. A single life can hold some of all three: a line you won't cross, a place where you're trying to be salt, and two sets of duties you carry at once.
screen: `NOT OUT OF THE WORLD, BUT KEPT.`
`CHANGE IT: THE SALT OF THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Walk through the places you'll be in the next few days, work, home, a screen, a store, maybe a church, and in each one ask quietly: where do I blend in here, and where do I live a little differently? Don't grade the answers; just notice. If you pray, you can hold those places before God one by one.
Christ and culture. How Christians live inside the wider world: set apart, working to change it, or as citizens of two kingdoms at once.
Your line: in the world, not of it. Not taken out, but kept. See you tomorrow.

1232.title: Open doors
1232.hook: Christian hospitality: the Lord's table, and our kitchen tables
1232.howItsDone: Christians practice hospitality at the Lord's table in worship and at home, sharing meals with neighbors, newcomers and people in need; some congregations also run community meals and coffee hours open to anyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ and culture, three ways to live in the world. Your line was in the world, not of it.

It's the heat of the day, and Abraham is sitting in the doorway of his tent. He looks up, and three men are standing nearby. Genesis tells what happens next, and most of it is running. He runs to meet them. He bows to the ground. He hurries into the tent and asks Sarah to bake bread. He runs to the herd and picks out a calf. Then, the King James Bible says, "he stood by them under the tree, and they did eat." The story has already said who came to that meal: the Lord appeared to him there. Today closes a week, and it ends at a door left open, at the tent this path first visited on day three hundred fifty-three.
screen: `HE STOOD BY THEM, AND THEY DID EAT.`

segments.voice: The letter to the Hebrews says: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Some readers hear Abraham's tent behind that line. The guests aren't old friends. They're strangers. The Greek word Hebrews uses is philoxenia, and the King James turns it into a whole phrase: to entertain strangers. The first letter of Peter adds a condition that's harder than it sounds: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Open the door, and don't keep score of what it costs. Christians carry this to two tables. One is the Lord's table, communion. Churches differ on what happens there and who may receive: some invite every baptized believer, others ask that those who receive share that church's full faith. This path ranks none of them. The other is the kitchen table. And the door swings both ways. In Revelation, Christ says: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." Look back at this week. Medicine, healing through human hands. Attention, guarding what we look at. Forgiveness that doesn't mean staying in danger. Going to your brother privately first. Blessing enemies. In the world, not of it. And now an open door. Every one of them is about how a life meets other people.
screen: `I STAND AT THE DOOR, AND KNOCK.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who could use a seat at your table, someone new in town, someone alone, and strip the invitation down: not a dinner party, just a cup of coffee or a bowl of soup. Notice what argues back, the mess, the time, the fear of awkward silence, and keep the picture of the open door. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.
Open doors. Christian hospitality, from Abraham's tent to the Lord's table to an ordinary kitchen, offered first of all to strangers.
Your line: an open door. The house doesn't have to be clean first. That closes the week.

chat.says: Hospitality just means hosting friends for nice dinners, right?
options: Not quite. Hebrews says entertain strangers, and Peter says without grudging. Soup counts.
Right. Hebrews says to host your old friends often, so none of them feel forgotten.
Right. Peter says to keep careful track of the cost, and host only when you can afford it.
